blocks.html: About Us

SurgicGuide Limited is a biotech company based in Hong Kong. Our aim is to advance novel technologies for precision cancer surgery. Our research focuses on using Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging Microscopy (FLIM) as a tool for distinguishing tumours from normal tissues.  By combining FLIM with artificial intelligence (AI), our cutting-edge technology provides surgeons with real-time guidance in tumour resection, thereby reducing the risk of positive surgical margins and tumour recurrence.

By integrating FLIM with machine learning, surgical efficiency can be remarkably improved, enabling hospitals to treat more patients despite limited clinical capacity.

blocks.html: AI-integrated FLIM System
Challenges of tumour resection

Cancer is a life-threatening disease that is very difficult to treat because of the recurrence after surgical resection. Cancer surgeries are challenging because a ‘complete’ resection may risk damaging surrounding tissue and affecting organ function, whereas a safer and more cautious approach is often followed by tumour recurrence, so patients must undergo follow-up treatments like chemotherapy or second stage surgery (22). More fundamentally, tumour boundaries are often indistinguishable to the naked eye, and smaller lesions can easily remain obscured during surgery. These factors all contribute to the high recurrence rate of cancer.

blocks.html: Current solution: image-guided surgery

Several imaging modalities are currently available to provide intraoperative surgical guidance, including ultrasound imaging, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT) and fluorescence imaging. Although these tools are in use for tumour delineation, most of them are constrained by the following clinical limitations (23, 24):

​

  • Sophisticated modalities like MRI and CT require specialized technologists

​

  • Maintenance of MRI and CT scanners are expensive, which limits their accessibility

​

  • The guidance provided by images is very limited, the determination of resection margin is highly dependent on surgeon’s experience and interpretation

​

  • Intraoperative scanning and subsequent image processing are time-consuming, so the guidance is technically not in real time, causing delay in surgery

​

  • Most images are qualitative, they are not linked to any absolute biochemical measurements, so the information provided from the images is limited.

rich.comp-mjpvk9yd: NAD(P)H as an indicator of metabolism
rich.comp-mjpvgy7h: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP+) are electron carriers crucial to human metabolism. They exist in equilibrium with their reduced form, NADH and NADPH respectively. Together, NADH and NADPH are called NAD(P)H (1). The biological pathways that are coupled to the redox of NAD(P)H are summarised in the diagrams below.
rich.comp-mjqv61ry: Compared to normal cells, cancer cells preferentially use glycolysis rather than oxidative phosphorylation for ATP production despite the presence of oxygen, which is known as the Warburg effect (2), The Warburg effect is one of the phenomenon that shows cancer cells modify their metabolism to support proliferation. Although the Warburg effect was rationalised by benefits such as promoting ATP synthesis and biosynthesis, it does not fully explain the metabolism in cancer cell (3).
rich.comp-mjqw9lmj:
The Warburg effect is characterised by increased glycolytic flux and increased NAD+ demand, which is supported by mechanisms including malate-aspartate shuttle and lactate fermentation (4). Furthermore, adaptation of cancer cells also include shift in biosynthetic pathways and reactive oxygen species production (5), so both NADH and NADPH level are affected.


Moreira et al. found that the [NAD+]/[NADH] and [NADP+]/[NADPH] ratios are increased approximately fivefold and tenfold in cancer cells relative to normal cells (6). 

​

Potential Rationale:​​

  • In order to maintain high glycolytic rate in cancer cells, pyruvate needs to be rapidly removed, while NAD+ needs to be rapidly replenished. This is achieved by the expression of lactate dehydrogenase, which couples the reduction of pyruvate with the oxidation of NADH, resulting in a high [NAD+]/[NADH] ratio that maintains the glycolytic flux (7).

​

  • The high [NADP+]/[NADPH] ratio can be attributed to the increased use of NADPH as a reducing agent for generation of antioxidant defence and anabolic reactions such as nucleotide, amino acid and fatty acid synthesis (8).
rich.comp-mjqyrqwg: Distinguish cancer tissues from normal tissues
rich.comp-mjqyrqwj:
Although the Warburg effect is not a universal phenomenon for all cancer types, it has been shown consistently that the metabolism and microenvironment cancer cells is significantly different from normal cells. These affect the properties of fluorescence molecules.


Since NAD(P)H is intrinsically fluorescent (9), whereas its oxidised forms are not, fluorescence imaging allows the redox state to be assessed without using any exogenous fluorescence probes. Research has shown that brain tumour tissues emit lower autofluorescence intensity than normal tissues, so fluorescence imaging could allow delineation of tumour resection margin (10-12). However, the clinical application of this intensity-based approach is constrained by significant limitations:

​

  • Non-uniform illumination artefacts: The fluorescence image is bright at the centre, but intensity drops at the periphery due to uneven illumination of endoscope (12)

​

  • Low sensitivity: NAD(P)H has low quantum yield, so fluorescence image has low signal to noise ratio due to background fluorescence (13)

​

  • Haemoglobin absorption: fluorescence intensity signals are attenuated by haemoglobin, so blood vessels in tissue may affect discrimination between tumour and normal tissue (14)
rich.comp-mjqzqoiz: Figure: Fluorescence intensity image of normal cortex (left) and glioblastoma (right). (Sun et al., 2010)
rich.comp-mjr05q8e: Application of FLIM in cancer surgery
rich.comp-mjr05q8h:
In contrast to fluorescence intensity measurements, fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) provides a robust metric for delineating tumour resection margin.

​

Fluorescence lifetime is the duration in which a fluorophore stays in its excited state before returning to the ground state. The fluorescence lifetime of a fluorophore is largely determined by the non-radiative decay rate, in other words, the restraint of molecular motion. For example, low temperature, high viscosity or a protein-bound state hinders non-radiative relaxation, thereby increases the fluorescence lifetime. Therefore, fluorescence lifetime is very sensitive to microenvironment and metabolic states.​

** Please check the Science for non-specialists page for the basics of FLIM

​

It has been demonstrated that FLIM enabled discrimination between glioblastoma and normal cortex with a high statistical significance (p = 0.0027), more robust than intensity-based imaging (p = 0.0199) (12).
rich.comp-mjra4ro8: Figure: Fluorescence lifetime image of normal cortex (left) and glioblastoma (right). (Sun et al., 2010)
rich.comp-mjraec6l:
The robustness of FLIM is largely attributed to the fact that fluorescence lifetime is an intrinsic property, independent of NAD(P)H concentration and the detected intensity (15). Therefore, fluorescence lifetime remains uniform across the field of view, unaffected by background lighting.

​

Furthermore, fluorescence lifetime is influenced by various parameters that differentiate tumour from normal tissues. For example, the free and protein-bound states of NAD(P)H have distinct fluorescence lifetimes, and the free to bound ratio of NADH is linked to [NAD+]/[NADH] ratio (16, 17). In addition, the fluorescence lifetime of enzyme-bound NADH and NADPH are different and the lifetimes depend on enzyme binding configuration and which enzyme NAD(P)H is bound (18, 19). Therefore, the metabolic and environmental change in cancer compared to normal tissue results in the measurable difference in fluorescence lifetime, making FLIM a sensitive surgical tool.

blocks.text: In contrast to fluorescence intensity measurements, fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) provides a robust metric for delineating tumour resection margin. ​ Fluorescence lifetime is the duration in which a fluorophore stays in its excited state before returning to the ground state. The fluorescence lifetime of a fluorophore is largely determined by the non-radiative decay rate, in other words, the restraint of molecular motion. For example, low temperature, high viscosity or a protein-bound state hinders non-radiative relaxation, thereby increases the fluorescence lifetime. Therefore, fluorescence lifetime is very sensitive to microenvironment and metabolic states. ​ ** Please check the Science for non-specialists page for the basics of FLIM ​ It has been demonstrated that FLIM enabled discrimination between glioblastoma and normal cortex with a high statistical significance ( p = 0.0027), more robust than intensity-based imaging ( p = 0.0199) (12).

blocks.html: Figure: Fluorescence lifetime image of normal cortex (left) and glioblastoma (right). (Sun et al., 2010)
blocks.text: Figure: Fluorescence lifetime image of normal cortex (left) and glioblastoma (right). (Sun et al., 2010)

blocks.html:
The robustness of FLIM is largely attributed to the fact that fluorescence lifetime is an intrinsic property, independent of NAD(P)H concentration and the detected intensity (15). Therefore, fluorescence lifetime remains uniform across the field of view, unaffected by background lighting.

​

Furthermore, fluorescence lifetime is influenced by various parameters that differentiate tumour from normal tissues. For example, the free and protein-bound states of NAD(P)H have distinct fluorescence lifetimes, and the free to bound ratio of NADH is linked to [NAD+]/[NADH] ratio (16, 17). In addition, the fluorescence lifetime of enzyme-bound NADH and NADPH are different and the lifetimes depend on enzyme binding configuration and which enzyme NAD(P)H is bound (18, 19). Therefore, the metabolic and environmental change in cancer compared to normal tissue results in the measurable difference in fluorescence lifetime, making FLIM a sensitive surgical tool.

blocks.html: What is fluorescence?

When a fluorescent molecule (fluorophore) absorbs a photon at a specific excitation wavelength, it transitions from ground state to excited states. The fluorophore may return to the ground state through radiative decay by emitting a photon with longer wavelength (fluorescence), or through non-radiative decay, which releases the energy without emitting a photon.

blocks.html: What is FLIM?

Fluorescence lifetime is the average time in which a fluorophore spent in its excited state before emitting fluorescence. Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) works like a stopwatch, which measures the time delay between a laser pulse and the detection of the resulting fluorescence (Fig A). It takes multiple measurements to generate a histogram that shows photon count as a function of time (Fig B). The fluorescence lifetime is determined by fitting the histogram with an exponential decay. A FLIM image is a pseudo-color map where each pixel represents an average fluorescence lifetime (Fig C). 

​

In general, fluorescence lifetime of a molecule depends on pH, viscosity, ion concentration and temperature of the local environment..

blocks.html: Tumour margin delineation with FLIM

In simplified terms, cancer cells reprogramme their glucose metabolism, leading to changes in cellular microenvironment and the composition of fluorescence molecules including NAD(P)H and FAD. Therefore, the fluorescence lifetimes of cancer and normal tissues are significantly different. This allows FLIM to delineate tumour margin, thereby guiding tumour resection in surgery.
